title.en: Cochinango: The Ass, the Buyo, and the Dancing Guitar
title.zh: 科奇南戈：驢、檳榔與舞曲吉他

region.en: Laoag, Ilocos Norte, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's grandmother's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋北伊洛克斯省佬沃（敘述者祖母故鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango', eBook #8299

summary.en: A palmer foretells that the 'fool' Cochinango will dine with the king, kiss the princess, marry her, and be king. Kindness on the road wins him a question-answering buyo, a food-furnishing cane, an inexhaustible purse, and — for his ass — a guitar that makes anyone dance. Winning the princess's riddle-contest earns only prison; but the cane feeds his fellow-prisoners, the purse buys his dinner with the king, and a night of inescapable guitar music wins the marriage — after which his dancing enemies save the kingdom from raiding Moros.
summary.zh: 朝聖者預言：被喚作『傻瓜』的科奇南戈終將與王共餐、親吻公主、娶她為妻、繼而為王。一路行善，他先後得能答萬問的檳榔、予食的拐杖、取之不竭的錢袋，並以毛驢換得令人起舞的吉他。贏了猜謎卻被囚；拐杖餵飽獄友，錢袋換來御宴，一曲通宵達旦的吉他迫使國王允婚——此後他以舞曲退摩洛海寇，繼位為王。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Velasco narrator (grandmother from Laoag); archival record. The magic buyo is likely native Ilocano belief or Tinguian-influenced (Fansler); the closing reference to raiding Moros 'appears to be a remnant of very old native tradition.'

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in a small village on the border of a powerful kingdom a poor farmer who had a son. This son was called a fool by many; but a palmer predicted that Cochinango would some day dine with the king, kiss the princess, marry her, and finally would himself be king. Cochinango wondered how he could ever marry the princess and himself be king, for he was very poor — until one day he heard that the king had summoned all those who would like to attempt to answer the questions of the princess, the person who could answer them all without fail to marry her; so he mounted his ass and rode toward the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On his way Cochinango had to pass through a wide forest, where he met a weary traveller and asked him for buyo, having forgotten to bring any; the traveller gave him a magic buyo that would answer any question he put to it, in exchange for food. At a stream he offered to carry across an old man too weak to swim, and in return received his cane, which would furnish food at any time — and this old man was the same one who had given him the magic buyo: it was God himself, who had come down on earth to test Cochinango and to reward him for his kindness. Then, out of pity, he gave a centavo to a wretched old woman and received an empty purse from which he could ask any sum of money he wanted; and God, again in the form of a jolly young fellow with a small guitar, asked him to exchange his ass for the guitar, since he could make anybody dance by plucking its strings. Cochinango had to proceed on foot, and it took him two days to reach the gates of the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Luckily he arrived on the very day of the guessing-contest, and in spite of his mean dress he was admitted. The princess was much astonished at Cochinango's appearance and disgusted by his boldness — but she was even more chagrined when he rightly answered her first question; she denied that his answer was correct, and asked him two more questions, the most difficult she could think of, but Cochinango, with the help of his magic buyo, answered both. She shrunk from the idea of being married to a poor, foolish, lowly-born man, and asked her father the king to imprison the insolent peasant, which was instantly done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the prison Cochinango found many nobles who, like himself, were victims of the guessing-match; night came, and they were given no food, for the princess wanted to starve them to death. Cochinango told them not to worry: he struck a table with his cane, and instantly choice food appeared. When this was reported to the princess she went to the prison and begged Cochinango to give her the cane; but he would not give it up unless she allowed him to kiss her. At last she consented and went away with the cane, thinking this was the only way she could starve her prisoners — but the next day Cochinango asked a large sum of money from his magic purse, distributed it among his companions and the guards, and they had no difficulty in getting food. Again the princess went to the prison and asked for the purse; he would give it up only on condition that he be allowed to dine with the king — and accordingly he was taken to the king's table, where he ate with the king and the princess, though he was put in prison again as soon as the dinner was over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Cochinango began to be tired of prison life, so he took up his wonderful guitar and began to play it: no sooner had he touched the strings than his fellow-prisoners and the guards began to dance; he played louder and louder, and the inmates of the palace heard it and they too began to dance; he kept on playing throughout the night, and the king, princess, and all got no rest whatsoever — by morning most of them were tired to death. At last the king ordered the guards to open the prison doors and let the prisoners go free; but Cochinango would not stop playing until the king consented to give him the princess in marriage, and the princess also at last had to agree to accept Cochinango as her husband. The next day they were married with great pomp and ceremony. Thus the poor, foolish boy was married to a princess; more than once he saved the kingdom from the raiding Moros by playing his guitar, for all his enemies were obliged to dance when they heard the music, and thus they were easily captured or killed. When the king died, Cochinango became his successor, and he and the princess ruled happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 35 'Cochinango'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pedro and the Witch: The Red and White Handkerchiefs
title.zh: 佩德羅與巫婆：紅白兩巾

region.en: San Narciso, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋三描禮士省聖納爾西索（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Zambal oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch', eBook #8299

summary.en: Left alone at nightfall, Pedro opens the door to Boroka, the bird-winged, horse-footed witch with a woman's head who devours children's livers; obedient, he becomes her housekeeper and befriends a visiting horse. When children grow scarce and the witch plans to serve Pedro at a feast of witches, the horse gives him two handkerchiefs and carries him off — the red one becomes a fire that burns off the witches' wings, the white one a wide sea they cannot pass.
summary.zh: 夜幕中應門的佩德羅落入巫婆博羅卡之手——鳥翼馬足、人頭食童肝的怪物。他乖順地當起管家，並與常來探望的馬結為好友。孩童漸稀、巫婆擬以他為宴饗之時，馬兒贈他兩方手帕、載他狂奔：紅巾化烈火燒盡巫婆之翼，白巾化大海阻斷追兵。

sensitivity.note: Zambal tale recorded by Fansler from a Dumlao narrator (San Narciso, Zambales); archival record. Fansler regards it as the detritus of a literary tradition from Europe (the Pampangan corrido 'Pugut Negro' / Don Octavio cycle and the widely-known 'Juan Tiñoso'), noting Boroka is a native demon-name.

passages.text: Pedro was the son of a poor man; he lived with his father and mother by the seashore. Early one morning his parents went to look for food, leaving him alone in the house; he stayed there all day waiting for them to return. Evening came, but his father and mother did not appear — some misfortune had overtaken them. Pedro felt very hungry, but he could find no food in the house. In the middle of the night he heard someone tapping at the door; thinking that it was his mother, he arose and went to meet her — but when he opened the door, he saw that it was not his mother who had rapped, but Boroka, whom children are very much afraid of. Now, Boroka was a witch: she had wings like a bird, four feet like a horse, but a head like that of a woman. She devoured boys and girls, and was especially fond of their liver. As soon as Pedro opened the door, she seized him and carried him off to her home in the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pedro was not afraid of the witch; he was obedient to her, and soon she made him her housekeeper. Whenever she went out at night to look for food, he was sure to have flesh and liver for breakfast the next day. Whenever the witch was away, Pedro used to amuse himself riding on the back of a horse that would often come to see him; it taught him how to ride well, and the two became great friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when children began to get scarce, and Boroka was unable to find any to eat, she made up her mind to kill Pedro: she left the house and went to invite the other witches, so that they might have a great feast. While she was gone, the horse came and told Pedro of his danger, and advised him what to do; it gave him two handkerchiefs, one red and the other white. Then Pedro jumped on the horse's back, and the horse ran away as fast as it could. Not long afterward he noticed that the witches were pursuing them; when they came nearer, Pedro dropped the red handkerchief, which was immediately changed into a large fire — the wings of the witches were all burnt off. However, the witches tried to pursue the horse on foot, for they could run very fast; when they were almost upon him again, Pedro dropped the white handkerchief, which became a wide sea through which the witches could not pass. Pedro was now safe, and he thanked the horse for its great help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 36 'Pedro and the Witch'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman and Her Coles Plant

region.en: Batangas city, Luzon, Philippines (tale common there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁城（故事流行之地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral exemplum; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant', eBook #8299

summary.en: A beggar-woman's coles seed grows to the sky; climbing it she begs St. Peter for a wand that grants any wish, feasts on summoned tables — and grows so proud she no longer knows her friends. Demanding that the church bells toll for her, she is struck senseless by the swinging bell; recovering, she climbs again for another gift, but the plant breaks halfway to heaven and she is killed by her fall — punished for her vanity.
summary.zh: 乞婦種下甘藍，藤蔓直上雲霄。她攀至天界，向聖彼得求得『要什麼有什麼』的神杖，從此錦衣玉食、目中無友。她竟令教堂鐘為她而鳴——鐘錘當頭將她擊昏；醒後再度攀藤求賜，藤蔓半途折斷，她墜地而亡——虛榮之罰。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog exemplum recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Jack-and-the-Beanstalk machinery joined to the Fisherman-and-his-Wife moral; Fansler derives it from a French or Italian Märchen, probably through the clergy.

passages.text: Once there lived a very poor woman. She lived practically by begging, but sometimes she got money with which to buy rice by selling small vegetables in the market; she had a little garden, and one day planted some seeds. Out of one of these seeds there grew up a plant which we call coles: this plant grew very fast, and in a few months it reached the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of curiosity, one day the woman began to climb the plant; when she was assured that it was strong she kept on climbing, and did not stop until she reached the sky. There she called to St. Peter, and asked him to give her a magic wand from which she could ask anything she wished; St. Peter gave her what she asked for, but told her not to disturb him again. Then she descended, and went down so quickly that she almost hurt herself. When she reached her little hut, she at once asked the wand for food: immediately there appeared a table on which was the best food in the world; when she had finished eating, she commanded the table to disappear, and it disappeared instantly. Now she became very proud on account of her wonderful possession — she did not recognize her friends any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day an archbishop arrived in the town in which she was living, and all the bells were rung in his honor; she then became very angry, and wondered why the bells were not rung for her whenever she passed in front of the church. So she went to the tower where the bells were, and commanded them to toll for her. They began to ring — but she was struck on the head and was knocked senseless. When she recovered, she hastened home and began to climb the plant to ask St. Peter for another gift; but, before she had covered one-half the distance to the sky, the plant broke, and she was killed by her fall. Thus she was punished for her vanity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 37 'The Woman and her Coles Plant'; not verbatim.

title.en: A Negrito Slave: The Three Questions

region.en: Valladolid, Negros Occidental, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓西內格羅省瓦利亞多利德（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Visayan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave', eBook #8299

summary.en: A Negrito with a wish-granting ring whitens his skin, masks himself as his young master, and answers the princess-king's three questions in his place: God owns the kingdom; the king is worth thirty pieces of silver, like the Saviour; and he can drink all the fresh water in the world once the king separates it from the salt. The youngest prince marries the princess; the Negrito receives the maid of honor.
summary.zh: 有許願戒指的小黑奴以法美白膚、戴上酷似少主的面具代其應答三問：王國屬於上帝；國王值三十塊銀元——救主被賣的價錢；只要國王先把海水與淡水分開，他便能喝盡天下淡水。少年王子娶得公主，小黑奴則得女儐相為妻。

sensitivity.note: Visayan folktale recorded by Fansler from a de la Rama narrator (Valladolid, Negros Occidental); archival record. Fansler traces the three-questions cycle to Europe (Grimm No. 152, 'The King and the Bishop' family), the Negrito taking the miller's role; the record retains the period's colonial framing and naming, noted here.

passages.text: Once upon a time there were three princes who owned a Negrito slave; although he was called a slave he was not really one, for the princes, especially the youngest, whom he loved most, treated him kindly. One striking characteristic of this Negrito was that his grinning was like that of a monkey, and he often grinned without cause; he would often follow his young master when he went out for a walk, and he had a suit similar to the prince's, so that, when they were out on the street, they looked very much alike — the only difference was that he was black, and the prince was white. Yet he owned a ring, a charm which had been given him by a woman for saving her from the hands of a robber; this ring gave him power to call for anything he wanted, and this was the reason, doubtless, why he was treated with kindness by his masters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a neighboring land there was a king who had a beautiful daughter who wanted to marry; so desirous was she of having a companion that she could not sleep day or night, meditating on how she could have a husband that would suit both herself and her father. At last, won over by her many entreaties, the king proclaimed to all the world that his daughter would marry anyone who had a handsome appearance and who could answer his three difficult questions; those who came to the court and were unable to answer the questions of the king were to lose their lives. The three princes were all handsome; the two elder brothers tried to answer the king's questions, but lost their lives. The youngest remained, and although he wanted to try, he was sure he would fail too. The Negrito determined to help him: by means of his ring he was able to make his skin white, and he also got a mask that was exactly like the face of his young master; then he dressed himself to resemble the prince, and went to the court of the king. 'Will you have your head cut off, too?' said the king. 'Yes, if I cannot answer your questions; but let us see!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Who owns this kingdom?' 'God owns this kingdom.' The king was surprised at his bold reply; however, he could not say that it was not God's, for that would be untrue: therefore he could not compel the prince to answer that it was his. 'How much am I worth?' 'You are not worth more than thirty pieces of silver.' The king was furious, and said that, if the prince could not give a good reason for his insulting words, he would be put to death instantly. 'Yes, yes! Our Saviour was sold for that much: therefore you, who are inferior to the Saviour, cannot be worth more than he was sold for.' The people at the court were astounded, and murmured to one another, 'The prince is wise. He is wise, indeed!' 'Well, answer this third question, and you shall be married to my daughter: Can you drink all the fresh water in the world?' 'Yes... But here, in many parts of the world the water of the ocean mixes with the fresh water: so, before I drink, you must separate the fresh water from the salt.' As the king was unable to do this, he acknowledged himself vanquished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'All right. To-morrow come here for the wedding.' The Negrito hastened home and told his young master all that had happened; the prince gave him five thousand pesetas, and promised him that he would urge the princess to give her consent to the marriage of the Negrito with her maid of honor. The next morning the prince and the princess were married, and the following day the Negrito received the maid of honor for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 38 'A Negrito Slave'; not verbatim.
